title: Effective searching
examples: When I search for something, how do I find only pictures?
What does it mean to use an operator in a search?
Can you show me how to narrow down my search results?

explain.say: Today we are learning how to search better online.
First we use strong keywords to start our search.
Next we use special operators to make our search very specific.
Then we use filters to choose exactly what we want to see.
For example, if you search for dogs and cats, you can use quotes.
In real life, imagine you need to find only recipes for chocolate cake.

faq.q: What is the difference between keywords and operators?
faq.a: Keywords are the main words you type in. Operators are special symbols that tell the search engine how to use those words.
asks: How do I make my search words work together?
Are operators like grammar rules for searching?

faq.q: Can I use operators to exclude words?
faq.a: Yes, you can use an operator like a minus sign to tell the engine to ignore certain words. This helps clean up your results.
asks: How do I search for everything except one thing?
Is there a way to remove unwanted results?

faq.a: Filters help you narrow down the type of information you see, like only showing images or only showing news articles.
asks: Do filters change what I type?
Can I filter by date or location?

faq.q: If I use too many keywords, will my search fail?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but it might become too complicated. Start with a few strong keywords first.
asks: Is there a limit to how many words I can use?
When should I stop adding keywords?

faq.q: Do I need to use quotation marks always?
faq.a: No, you only need them when you want the search engine to treat a group of words as one exact phrase.
asks: What happens if I forget the quotes?

facts: Keywords are the core words describing your topic.
Operators like quotation marks force exact phrases.
Filters let you select the format, like images or videos.
Using all three together makes searching very precise.

quiz.say: I want to find information about the Great Pyramids of Giza, but only results that are pictures.
quiz.why: You must use the filter tool to limit results to only pictures.

wrong.0: Operators are specific symbols, and this is not a standard operator.
wrong.2: This only searches for the exact words, not the type of result.
wrong.3: This might find articles that mention the word picture, not just the images.

quiz.say: If I search for dogs and I want results that mention 'Golden Retriever' exactly, what should I do?

options.show: Use quotation marks around the phrase.
options.say: Use quotation marks around the phrase.

quiz.why: Quotation marks tell the engine to search for those words together in that order.

wrong.0: The AND operator is usually implied and doesn't require quotes.
wrong.1: This is okay, but quotes are better for guaranteeing the exact phrase.
wrong.2: The plus sign is not a universal operator for exact phrases.

quiz.say: I am researching photosynthesis. I want to find results about 'plant energy' but I do not want any results mentioning 'animal'.

options.show: Use a minus sign operator before the unwanted word.
options.say: Use a minus sign operator before the unwanted word.

options.show: Search for photosynthesis plant energy and then delete animal results
options.say: Search for photosynthesis plant energy and then delete animal results

options.show: Use quotes around 'animal' to exclude it
options.say: Use quotes around 'animal' to exclude it

quiz.why: The minus sign tells the search engine to exclude any page containing that word.

wrong.1: While logical, the minus sign is the standard, recognized operator.
wrong.2: This is too manual and not a search function.
wrong.3: Quotes search for the phrase, they do not function as an exclusion tool.
